# VASO, Multi-echo, and MR Fingerprinting

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

---

This chapter collects three more methods. VASO is a functional contrast that
isolates blood volume rather than blood oxygenation. Multi-echo acquisition
turns the ordinary T2\* signal into separate estimates of the starting
magnetization and the decay time. MR fingerprinting abandons the idea of a
single contrast entirely, using a deliberately varied acquisition and
pattern-matching to read out several tissue parameters at once.

## VASO

Vascular-space-occupancy (VASO) imaging, developed by van Zijl and colleagues,
is a functional method aimed at improving the spatial specificity of fMRI
(@fig-ch64-vaso-concept). It exploits the fact that the T1 of blood differs from
the T1 of brain parenchyma. By timing an inversion pulse to null the blood
signal, VASO suppresses the contribution from within the vessels while sparing
the tissue signal. Changes in the nulled signal then track changes in blood
*volume*, a different physiological variable than the blood-oxygenation change
that drives BOLD.

![VASO uses an inversion pulse timed to null the blood signal — possible because
blood and parenchyma have different T1 — so that the measured change reflects
blood volume.](images/ch64/vaso-concept.png){#fig-ch64-vaso-concept}

## Multi-echo imaging

An ordinary gradient-echo measures the signal at a single echo time, so the
value it reports mixes two things: the starting magnetization S₀ (set by proton
density and by transmit/receive coil sensitivity) and the T2\* decay. That is
why a plain T2\*-weighted image is not quantitative — the absolute signal level
at a given echo time differs from place to place even when the underlying decay
constant is the same (@fig-ch64-multiecho-t2-not-quantitative). What is
comparable across locations is the *time constant* of the decay, not the signal
level at one instant.

![The measured signal at a fixed echo time depends on both S₀ and T2\*. Because
proton density and coil inhomogeneity make S₀ vary across the brain, the signal
level is not comparable between locations; the T2\* time constant
is.](images/ch64/multiecho-t2-not-quantitative.png){#fig-ch64-multiecho-t2-not-quantitative}

Multi-echo acquisition addresses this by reading out the same excitation at
several echo times (@fig-ch64-multiecho-examples). Fitting the exponential decay
across echoes separates the two quantities, producing an S₀ map and a T2\* map
(@fig-ch64-multiecho-s0-t2star-maps). This separation is valuable for
denoising functional data: BOLD is nominally a T2\* change, but real signals
also contain S₀ fluctuations that are artifactual, and having both maps lets one
be removed to clean up the other.

![The same slice acquired at increasing echo times (TE = 15, 31, 48 ms). The
contrast changes systematically with echo time as the signal
decays.](images/ch64/multiecho-examples.png){#fig-ch64-multiecho-examples}

![Fitting the decay across echoes yields separate S₀ and T2\* maps from the same
multi-echo data.](images/ch64/multiecho-s0-t2star-maps.png){#fig-ch64-multiecho-s0-t2star-maps}

## MR fingerprinting

MR fingerprinting (MRF), introduced by Ma and colleagues (Ma et al., 2013,
*Nature*), inverts the usual logic of an MR experiment. Rather than tuning the
sequence to produce one contrast, MRF drives the tissue with a deliberately
varied, pseudo-random sequence so that each tissue type produces a distinctive
signal "fingerprint" over time. Matching each measured fingerprint against a
precomputed dictionary of simulated signals then yields several tissue
parameters at once — T1, T2, and others — and, because the matching tolerates
imperfections, it suppresses measurement error rather than propagating it
(@fig-ch64-mrf-abstract).

![The MR fingerprinting proposal: a single varied acquisition, matched against
simulated signals, quantifies multiple tissue properties
simultaneously.](images/ch64/mrf-abstract.png){#fig-ch64-mrf-abstract}

In practice the acquisition is an ordinary pulse sequence — RF pulses, slice
selection, and a readout — but with the flip angle and repetition time changed
from one excitation to the next, and an efficient (often spiral) k-space
trajectory (@fig-ch64-mrf-pulse-sequence). The key design choice is the
*schedule* of flip angles and repetition times: a pseudo-random schedule
(@fig-ch64-mrf-concept) makes different tissues follow visibly different signal
trajectories.

![An MRF acquisition. The flip angle and repetition time vary across
excitations, read out along a spiral k-space
trajectory.](images/ch64/mrf-pulse-sequence.png){#fig-ch64-mrf-pulse-sequence}

![The flip-angle and repetition-time schedules are pseudo-random. Two example
schedules are shown; the varied parameters are what give each tissue a
distinctive signal.](images/ch64/mrf-concept.png){#fig-ch64-mrf-concept}

The readout step is a simulation-and-match. The expected signal trajectory for
each candidate substrate — white matter, gray matter, CSF, fat, off-resonance
variants — is simulated in advance, and the measured signal is assigned to
whichever simulated trajectory it matches best (@fig-ch64-mrf-simulation-match).
The same simulation-based reconstruction idea has been used more narrowly to get
fast, accurate quantitative T2 maps from multi-spin-echo data, correcting for
the stimulated and indirect echoes that otherwise contaminate rapid protocols.

![Different substrates produce distinct simulated signals (top); the measured
signal is matched to the best-fitting simulated trajectory
(bottom).](images/ch64/mrf-simulation-match.png){#fig-ch64-mrf-simulation-match}
